content: Tetanus is a serious and potentially life-threatening disease that can be effectively prevented through vaccination. However, in many developing countries, vaccination coverage remains suboptimal, leading to continued cases of tetanus. Even in developed countries, tetanus cases still occur, particularly among elderly individuals, due to their diminished immune protection. Globally, it is estimated that approximately 1 million cases of tetanus occur annually. Animal studies have demonstrated that vitamin C can provide protection against various infections and bacterial toxins. Specifically, in a study conducted on rats, vitamin C was shown to protect against the purified tetanus toxin. This has led to interest in exploring whether vitamin C could have a prophylactic or therapeutic role in human tetanus cases. To investigate this, a systematic review was conducted to assess the potential preventive and therapeutic effects of vitamin C on tetanus. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and Ovid EMBASE, was performed in May 2013. The review included controlled trials, regardless of whether they were placebo-controlled, and considered studies published in any language, whether published or unpublished. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies for inclusion and extracted data from the trial reports. Methodological quality was also evaluated. The analysis involved statistical methods to calculate odds ratios (ORs) and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For one dataset where a cell in a 2 × 2 table had no events, the Peto method was used to calculate the OR and its 95% CI. For another dataset with no empty cells, the inverse-variance method was applied to estimate the RR and its 95% CI. Additionally, Fisher's exact test was used to calculate the exact 95% CI for the OR in the table with the empty cell. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria for this review. This was a non-randomised, unblinded, controlled trial conducted in Bangladesh, involving 117 patients diagnosed with tetanus. In this study, vitamin C was administered intravenously at a dose of 1 gram per day in addition to standard conventional treatment. Participants were stratified into two age groups at the time of recruitment, and the results were reported separately for each group. The findings revealed a significant difference in the effect of vitamin C between the two age groups (P = 0.01). Among tetanus patients aged 1 to 12 years (n = 62), vitamin C treatment was associated with a 100% reduction in the case fatality rate (95% CI: -100% to -94%). In contrast, among patients aged 13 to 30 years (n = 55), vitamin C treatment was associated with a 45% reduction in the case fatality rate (95% CI: -69% to -5%). The authors concluded that this single, non-randomised, and poorly reported trial suggests that vitamin C may significantly reduce mortality in tetanus patients. However, due to concerns about the methodological quality of the trial, these results should be interpreted with caution. Based on the current evidence, vitamin C cannot be recommended as a treatment for tetanus. Further high-quality trials are needed to evaluate the potential role of vitamin C in the treatment of tetanus.
